The treatment of staphy- lococcal endocarditis is based on the use of an isoxa- zolyl penicillin or a glycopeptide. In contrast to strepto- coccal or enterococcal endocarditis, the benefits of adding an aminoglycoside are uncertain, and guidelines differ in whether they recommend this. Combination therapy is recommended where prosthetic valves or oth- er intracardiac prostheses are present. For meticillin sensitive staphylococci, typically cloxa- cillin, dicloxacillin, or flucloxacillin is given in a dose of 2 g every 4 to 6 hours for at least 4 weeks.4-8 Some guidelines continue to recommend addition of gen- tamicin for the first 3 to 5 days of therapy.7,8 Patients with right-sided endocarditis due to intravenous drug abuse may respond to shorter courses of 2 weeks of combination therapy with an isoxazolyl penicillin plus gentamicin.4,6-8 For staphylococci resistant to meticillin/oxacillin, van- comycin may be given alone for 6 weeks,4,7,8 or with rifampicin or perhaps gentamicin or sodium fusidate (depending on sensitivity) for at least 4 weeks.5-8 Such combinations may also be appropriate in patients with penicillin allergy. Teicoplanin should not be used as the reported incidence of treatment failure is unacceptably high.6 For staphylococcal endocarditis in the presence of int- racardiac prostheses either an isoxazolyl penicillin or vancomycin may be used with rifampicin or gentamicin or both; an indicative regimen might be intravenous doses of 2 g of the penicillin every 4 to 6 hours, or 1 g of vancomycin every 12 hours, plus rifampicin 300 mg by mouth every 8 hours, both given for 6 to 8 weeks, plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours for the first 2 weeks.6-8 Gentamicin may be given for the entire period of treatment if the infection is due to more recal- citrant strains of meticillin-resistant Staph. aureus or co- agulase-negative staphylococci.6 • Enterococcal endocarditis.
